Acțiune Facebook X WhatsApp Telegram VK Two high school graduates from the Romanian city of Bacău who achieved perfect scores in the 2026 national Baccalaureate examination will each receive a 3,000 lei cash award under a decision adopted by the Bacău City Council. The measure was approved during the City Council meeting on July 20 as part of a proposal to recognize outstanding academic performance in the June–July 2026 Baccalaureate session. The recipients are Anais Pesa-Moza , a graduate of Ferdinand I National College, and Delia-Andreea Nașcu , a graduate of Vasile Alecsandri National College. They were the only students in Bacău to complete the national examination with a perfect final grade of 10. During the council debate, Liberal Party (PNL) councillor Ilie Birzu proposed increasing the award from the initially planned 1,000 lei to 2,000 lei for each graduate. A subsequent amendment submitted by a Green Party councillor raised the amount to 3,000 lei, a proposal that was approved by the council. Local authorities said the initiative is intended to recognize academic excellence and reward the exceptional achievements of the two graduates in one of Romania’s most important national examinations. The Baccalaureate exam is the nationwide school-leaving examination required for admission to higher education in Romania. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.text: Image caption, Defence Minister Guido Crosetto has warned against showing any weakness to Russia's Vladimir Putin By Sarah Rainsford Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent ,Â Reporting from Rome Published 2 hours ago Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks. In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace. US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine. Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US. Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine. Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices. Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table. "Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome. Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war. "If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side â and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness â then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned. "I think that is completely wrong." Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Italy's prime minister has become a close ally of Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid. The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified. In our interview, the defence minister vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached. The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners. Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace' Published 10 hours ago Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role Published 10 hours ago That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground. At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian". Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with". But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia. "When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said. But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy. During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education. Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs." In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices. Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the IxÃ¨ institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%. There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too. But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow â targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia". "In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued. "It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining." Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe. The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity". A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us. But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response. "You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said. With additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwdd.text: Image source, Getty Images By Michael Race ,Â Business reporter Â and Â Simon Jack ,Â Business editor Published 3 hours ago The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China. Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in". He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market. A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy. The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations. It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels. There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey. Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures. "Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia. "Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help. "I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union." The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50â60%. The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years". "Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine. Image caption, Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer. But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment. All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently". At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added. Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began. Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids. "The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks." "Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged." Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history". "We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive." https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/andoni-ir.text: Oli Gent Tue, October 13, 2026 at 5:30 PM UTC 0 Liverpool are set to take on LASK in the Champions League on Wednesday, but they are sweating over the fitness of three big stars. Andoni Iraola was missing Dominik Szoboszlai , Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo for the heavy 3-0 defeat by Manchester City at Anfield on Sunday, as the Reds made a losing return to Premier League action. Lewis Koumas started up top for the Reds, while Bradley Barcola and Victor Munoz operated off the flanks, with Hugo Ekitike also sidelined with his pre-existing Achilles issue. Szoboszlai was a surprise exclusion from the matchday squad over the weekend, but it was revealed that the Hungarian had suffered a tight hamstring during the international break. Gakpo and Isak were out with ankle and thigh problems respectively. Now, the Reds are looking to follow up their 2-1 win over Atletico Madrid in their opening league phase encounter with a victory in Austria, but will they have any of their three big names back? “They are not bad but it's difficult to tell right now [when they will be back],” the Spaniard said on Tuesday. “We are taking it day to day. Really the three of them, I don't know if it's going to be Brentford or Villarreal.” As such, it means that the trio will not travel to LASK, but they could make the trip to the capital at the weekend, when the Reds visit the Gtech Community Stadium to face Brentford. After that, they host Villarreal in the Champions League before two quick-fire home games against Brighton and Hove Albion in then Chelsea in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.
